questions.text: Which pair has the same dimensions?
questions.feedback: Impulse is F·Δt = (M L T⁻²)(T) = M L T⁻¹; momentum is m·v = M · L T⁻¹. Identical — which is exactly why impulse changes momentum.

questions.text: A student derives that the speed of a wave on a string is v = √(T/μ), where T is tension (N) and μ is mass per length (kg/m). Does it pass a dimension check?
options: No — the units come out as kg
No — the units come out as m/s²
Can't tell without knowing the string
questions.feedback: N ÷ (kg/m) = (kg·m/s²)(m/kg) = m²/s². Square root: m/s. The formula is dimensionally sound (and correct).

questions.text: The Mars Climate Orbiter was lost because two teams used different units for:
questions.feedback: One system output pound‑force·seconds; the other expected newton·seconds. Same dimension (M L T⁻¹), different unit, factor of 4.45 — enough to drop the orbit into the atmosphere.

questions.text: Which of these is a base SI unit?
questions.feedback: The kilogram is defined directly. Newton and joule are named recipes of kg, m and s; the liter isn't SI at all (it's 10⁻³ m³).

questions.text: You need a time, and the problem gives you a height h (m) and g (m/s²). Before any algebra, the combination that yields seconds is:
questions.feedback: m ÷ (m/s²) = s², and a square root gives s. Dimensional analysis hands you the form of the answer — the actual √(2h/g) just adds the number.
